excerpt: If such additional facts are available, we have reason to believe that D is a mere partial ground that was misidentified as a full ground; in such a case, [p] instead is fully grounded in D, P. Each of the three cases set out above are such that additional explanatorily relevant facts are available that meet the modal entailment condition: what are identified as enabling conditions in the first case, a totality fact – the fact to the effect that a, b, etc. are everything that exists – in the second case, and the fact that Socrates and Xanthippe were married in the third case.
overview: The response to counterexamples explains how necessity can survive cases where an alleged ground does not entail its explanandum. Trogdon treats several examples as incomplete explanations: once enabling conditions, totality facts, or marriage facts are included, the modal entailment condition is restored. The strategy also leaves room for diagnosing some alleged grounds as non-grounds rather than partial grounds.
title: Counterexample Diagnosis
